description: Thirty STAND-IN third-party skills for the skill-selection corpus (tests/fixtures/skill-selection-corpus.json, set "large"). They are not copies of any published skill: nothing here was fetched, and every description was written for this fixture, modelled on the kinds of skill the five default registry sources (lib/skill-registry.mjs) are publicly known to carry, in the usual "use this when ..." style and at a realistic length (200 to 900 characters). The ids have the form the registry gives an entry, `<source id>-<folder>`, and the name is the folder name, as a SKILL.md front matter usually has it; the folder names are written from memory and were not checked against the repositories, so an id here may not exist there. The `systemPrompt` is a one-line placeholder: the real texts are long and are read on demand, and selection does not look at them.

skills.name: pdf
skills.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. That covers reading or extracting text and tables from a PDF, merging several PDFs into one, splitting a PDF apart, rotating pages, adding a watermark, creating a new PDF, filling in a PDF form, encrypting or decrypting a file, pulling images out of it, and running OCR on scanned pages so that they can be searched. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks for a PDF as the result, use this skill.

skills.name: docx
skills.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit or otherwise work with Word documents (.docx files). Triggers include any mention of "Word doc", "word document" or ".docx", and requests for a professional document with formatting such as a table of contents, headings, page numbers or a letterhead. Also use it to extract or reorganise the content of a .docx file, to insert or replace images, to find and replace text, to work with tracked changes or comments, or to turn content into a polished Word document. Do not use it for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs or coding tasks that have nothing to do with producing a document.

skills.name: xlsx
skills.description: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the main input or output. That means opening, reading, editing or fixing an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .csv or .tsv file (adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data), creating a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data, or converting between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user refers to a spreadsheet by name or path and wants something done to it or produced from it. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do not trigger when the main deliverable is a Word document, an HTML report, a standalone script or a database pipeline, even if tabular data is involved.

skills.name: pptx
skills.description: Use this skill any time a .pptx file is involved in any way, as input, as output or both. This includes creating slide decks, pitch decks or presentations; reading, parsing or extracting text from a .pptx file, even when the extracted content will be used elsewhere; editing or updating an existing presentation; combining or splitting slide files; and working with templates, layouts, speaker notes or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions a "deck", "slides" or a "presentation", or names a .pptx file, whatever they plan to do with the content afterwards.

skills.name: frontend-design
skills.description: Create distinctive, production-grade frontend interfaces with high design quality. Use this skill when the user asks to build web components, pages or applications: websites, landing pages, dashboards, React components, HTML/CSS layouts, or when styling and beautifying any web UI. It produces creative, polished code that avoids the generic look of machine-made interfaces, with deliberate choices of typography, colour, motion and layout.

skills.name: webapp-testing
skills.description: Toolkit for interacting with and testing local web applications using Playwright. Use it to verify frontend functionality, debug UI behaviour, capture browser screenshots and read browser console logs. It covers starting a local dev server, waiting for the page to settle, finding selectors on the rendered page, and writing short Python scripts that drive the browser against an app running on localhost.

skills.name: mcp-builder
skills.description: Guide for creating high-quality MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers that let a language model interact with external services through well-designed tools. Use when building an MCP server to integrate an external API or service, in Python (FastMCP) or in Node/TypeScript (the MCP SDK). It covers planning which tools to expose, naming them, input schemas, error messages that help the model, pagination, and how to write evaluations for the finished server.

skills.name: skill-creator
skills.description: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure how well a skill performs. Use when the user wants to create a skill from scratch, edit or optimise an existing skill, run evaluations to test a skill, benchmark it, or rewrite a skill's description so that it triggers more accurately. It explains the layout of a skill folder, the SKILL.md front matter, bundled scripts and reference files, and how to package the result.

skills.name: internal-comms
skills.description: A set of resources for writing all kinds of internal communications in the formats a company likes to use. Use this skill whenever asked to write some sort of internal communication: status reports, leadership updates, 3P updates (progress, plans, problems), company newsletters, FAQs, incident reports, project updates and announcements to a team or to the whole company.

skills.name: brand-guidelines
skills.description: Applies Anthropic's official brand colours and typography to any sort of artifact that may benefit from having Anthropic's look and feel. Use it when brand colours or style guidelines, visual formatting or company design standards apply: the colour palette with its hex values, the heading and body fonts and their fallbacks, and how to apply them to documents, slides and pages.

skills.name: canvas-design
skills.description: Create beautiful visual art in .png and .pdf documents using design philosophy. Use this skill when the user asks to create a poster, a piece of art, a design or another static piece. It first writes a short design philosophy and then expresses it on a canvas, with original visual work rather than a copy of an existing artist's style, and with very little text on the page.

skills.name: algorithmic-art
skills.description: Creating algorithmic art using p5.js with seeded randomness and interactive parameter exploration. Use this when users request creating art using code, generative art, algorithmic art, flow fields or particle systems. The result is an original piece expressed as a p5.js sketch in a single HTML page with controls for its parameters and its seed, rather than a copy of an existing artist's work.

skills.name: slack-gif-creator
skills.description: Knowledge and utilities for creating animated GIFs optimised for Slack. Provides the constraints (dimensions, frame rate, colour count and file size for an emoji and for a message), validation tools and animation concepts such as shake, bounce, spin and fade. Use when users request an animated GIF for Slack, for example "make me a GIF of X doing Y for Slack".

skills.name: theme-factory
skills.description: Toolkit for styling artifacts with a theme. These artifacts can be slides, documents, reports, HTML landing pages and so on. There are ten pre-set themes with colours and fonts that can be applied to any artifact that has been created, or a new theme can be generated on the fly from a short description. Use it when the user asks for a consistent theme, a colour scheme or a font pairing across an artifact.

skills.name: web-artifacts-builder
skills.description: Suite of tools for creating elaborate, multi-component HTML artifacts using modern frontend web technologies (React, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui). Use for complex artifacts that need state management, routing or shadcn/ui components, and not for simple single-file HTML or JSX artifacts. It initialises a project, lets you develop it, and bundles everything into one HTML file that can be shown as an artifact.

skills.name: gh-fix-ci
skills.description: Use when a user asks to debug or fix failing GitHub PR checks that run in GitHub Actions. Uses the gh command-line tool to inspect the checks of the pull request, fetch the logs of the failing job, summarise the failure, and propose a fix plan; it implements the fix only after the user approves the plan. External checks that do not run in GitHub Actions are out of scope: for those it only reports the link to their details page.

skills.name: gh-address-comments
skills.description: Help address review and issue comments on the open GitHub pull request of the current branch, using the gh command-line tool. It fetches every review thread and comment, numbers them with a short summary of what each asks for, asks the user which ones to address, and then applies the fixes for the chosen ones. Use it when the user asks to respond to reviewers, to address review feedback or to resolve the comments on a PR; make sure gh is authenticated first.

skills.name: security-best-practices
skills.description: Perform language and framework specific security best-practice reviews and suggest improvements. Trigger only when the user explicitly requests security best practices guidance, a security review or report, or secure-by-default coding help. Supported languages are Python, JavaScript/TypeScript and Go. It looks for injection, missing authentication and authorisation checks, unsafe deserialisation, weak session and cookie settings and similar problems, and writes the findings up by severity. Do not trigger for general code review, debugging or tasks that are not about security.

skills.name: playwright
skills.description: Use when the task requires automating a real browser from the terminal (navigation, form filling, snapshots, screenshots, data extraction, UI-flow debugging) with the Playwright command-line wrapper. It opens a page, takes a snapshot to find element references, clicks and types by reference, and takes a new snapshot after every navigation. Prefer it for checking a user interface by hand in a real browser; write a Playwright test file only when the user asks for tests.

skills.name: react-best-practices
skills.description: React and Next.js performance optimisation guidelines from Vercel Engineering. This skill should be used when writing, reviewing or refactoring React or Next.js code to make sure it follows the optimal performance patterns. Triggers on tasks that involve React components, Next.js pages, data fetching, bundle size or performance improvements: removing request waterfalls, reducing the bundle, server-side performance, client-side data fetching, re-render optimisation and rendering performance.

skills.name: web-design-guidelines
skills.description: Review UI code for compliance with the Web Interface Guidelines. Use when asked to "review my UI", "check accessibility", "audit design", "review UX" or "check my site against best practices". It fetches the current guidelines, reads the files the user names, and reports every finding as file and line: focus states, labels, keyboard support, contrast, motion, touch targets, forms and loading states.

skills.name: vercel-deploy
skills.description: Deploy applications and websites to Vercel. Use this skill when the user requests deployment actions such as "deploy my app", "deploy this to production", "create a preview deployment", "deploy and give me the link" or "push this live". No authentication is required: it packages the project, detects the framework, uploads it and returns a preview URL and a link with which the user can claim the deployment for their own account.

skills.name: git-commit
skills.description: Execute a git commit with a conventional commit message, intelligent staging and message generation. Use when the user asks to commit changes, to create a git commit, or mentions "/commit". It analyses the diff to decide the type and the scope of the message automatically, generates a conventional commit message from it, stages files in logical groups when asked, and never commits secrets or changes the git configuration.

skills.name: github-issues
skills.description: Create, update and manage GitHub issues. Use this skill when users want to create a bug report, a feature request or a task; to update an existing issue; to add labels, assignees or milestones; to triage a backlog by labelling, de-duplicating and closing issues; or to manage sub-issues and dependencies between issues. Triggers on requests like "create an issue", "file a bug", "request a feature", "triage the issues" or any other GitHub issue management task.

skills.name: code-review
skills.description: Review code changes for correctness, readability and maintainability before they are merged. Use when the user asks to review a diff, a pull request, a branch or a set of files, or asks "is this ready to merge?". It reads the change in the context of the surrounding code, looks for bugs, missing error handling, unclear naming and missing tests, and reports the findings in order of severity with the file and the line, keeping matters of taste apart from real defects.

skills.name: changelog-generator
skills.description: Generate a changelog or release notes from the history of a repository. Use when the user asks for a changelog, release notes, a "what's new" section or a summary of the changes between two tags or versions. It reads the commits and the merged pull requests since the previous release, groups them into features, fixes and breaking changes in the Keep a Changelog format, rewrites them in words a user of the product understands, and leaves out internal refactoring.

skills.name: github-actions-workflow
skills.description: Write and maintain GitHub Actions workflow files. Use when the user asks to create or change a workflow under .github/workflows: build, test and lint jobs on push and on pull requests, caching of dependencies, a build matrix, reusable workflows, secrets and environments, and publishing a release or a package. It follows the documented workflow syntax, keeps the permissions of the job token minimal and explains each trigger it adds.

skills.name: wrangler
skills.description: Cloudflare Workers CLI for deploying, developing and managing Workers, KV, R2, D1, Vectorize, Hyperdrive, Workers AI, Containers, Queues, Workflows, Pipelines and Secrets Store. Load before running wrangler commands to make sure the syntax and the best practices are right: the configuration file and its bindings, local development, deploying, tailing logs, secrets, and creating and migrating the storage products from the command line.

skills.name: workers-best-practices
skills.description: Reviews and authors Cloudflare Workers code against production best practices. Load when writing new Workers, reviewing Worker code, configuring wrangler.jsonc, or checking for common Workers anti-patterns such as streaming a whole body into memory, floating promises, global state that leaks between requests, secrets in the source and bindings that are used wrongly. It covers the request lifecycle, the limits of the runtime, observability and compatibility dates.

skills.name: durable-objects
skills.description: Create and review Cloudflare Durable Objects. Use when building stateful coordination (chat rooms, multiplayer games, booking systems), implementing RPC methods, SQLite storage, alarms or WebSockets, or reviewing Durable Object code for best practices. It covers the wrangler configuration and migrations, the storage interface, how to choose the key that names an object, and testing with the Workers test pool.
